utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everybody. Good afternoon, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Different but familiar setting. Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Let's start.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon to everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, to you, Mr. Donia. Mr. Donia, I'd like us to look at the period before the parties were established, briefly, and to see which points we agree upon so we don't have to debate them and go through documents that would be superfluous in that place. Now, in my books, and, you know, that I've written several books of poetry, a poetry book for children, a comedy and a novel. So in my books, did you ever come across anything that would indicate to you that -- what my state of consciousness was which would act against me in these proceedings, for instance?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't -- I'm not sure how to answer that. I have read some of your poetry, in particular, and I guess find there a particular style of expression which is really not something that I would say reveals a state of consciousness that would act against you in those proceedings, no. I wouldn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, have you read my novel, "The Magical Chronicle"?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately not, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, many of my books receive prizes and I'm not saying this from the literary point of view but from political correctness. All those books were awarded many prizes, from the Sholokhov prize, smaller ones, bigger ones, the Jovan Ducic prize, and so on and so forth. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about all the names that you just gave, but I know that you have won prizes and your literary works in general have been hailed by a good number of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, going back to the period before the Serb Democratic Party was formed. Do you know what my relationship was and attitude towards others and with others in the religious sense and national sense?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think you -- in the national sense you arrived in Sarajevo at the age of 15 from Montenegro and displayed, let's say, loyalty -- kind of a local loyalty to Montenegro which often expressed itself as a kind of a Serb loyalty. I think that changed a bit over time and became more of a Serb identity, at least as I -- as I understand it, and I'm obviously not able to speak to this like you are, but that in the course of the 1980s, in particular, as you went to Belgrade for several months and spent a year in prison that your Serb identity became more pronounced.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you agree that the area I came from in Montenegro up to the Berlin Congress was in Herzegovina and that to the present day it is called Old or Ancient Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, did you happen to note in the books of Vuk Karadzic that it says he's a -- from Herzegovina, Drobnjak, from Petnjica, and that is all my general area, the area I hailed from and my particular village?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Petnjica is indeed your home village and then you lived in Savnik for a while and moved to Niksic and finally to Sarajevo. So I'm aware of that and was not aware specifically of what Vuk Karadzic's association with that area was, but as I indicated earlier, recognise that his family and your family background intersect at some point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. His father was born in my village, in actual fact. Now, do you agree that by joining up with Montenegro we still -- we still remained Herzegovinian but with a great love for Montenegro, and that's why we joined up?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, joined up when or what -- to what did you join?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, Montenegro, at the Berlin Congress, was given independence, just like Serbia. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was, mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And Montenegro, at the time, was given many adjoining territories, and my territory, Old Herzegovina, united with Montenegro rather than remain in Herzegovina which was still under the Turks.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it -- Herzegovina was technically under Turkish sovereignty but under Austro-Hungarian administration after 1878. Demonstrably it wasn't then a part of Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But Old Herzegovina, which united with Montenegro, was no longer under Turk sovereignty as Herzegovina was until 1908. Herzegovina proper was under them. So do you agree that my Durmitor area and Old Herzegovina with a Serb population was conjoined with Montenegro, and it was free and that's why we united with it, because it was all Serb land anyway; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's a number of assertions there, some of which is -- I would -- I would question. The basic diplomatic outcome of the Congress of Berlin I don't argue with, but to say that these areas in Old Herzegovina were Serb land anyway, I wouldn't necessarily agree with that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But do you know anybody else who was a state? We call it St. Sava's land. But in any other state was the population anything other than Serb from time immemorial or from the Illyrians, let's say?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think we've been talking about Montenegro, and many Montenegrins would disagree with you about that statement and note that the land has been inhabited by Montenegrins for a long time. I would say it is a contested issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move away from Montenegro. But at that point, Montenegro was declared Serbian land and the population was that of Czar Nikola, King Nikola later on. He considered himself to be the Serb ruler.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Montenegro was not declared Serbian land at that time. It was declared an independent principality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, it was an independent state, but it was a Serb state, not part of Serbia but Serb land inhabited by the Serbs. But never mind that. My area was inhabited by a Serb population, and that when we joined up with Montenegro we did not lose our national identity. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was nothing about joining Montenegro that would have changed the national identity in that area, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I want us to throw more light on this, that my Serb national identity became slightly more marked in the 1980s, and we'll come to why in due course. But do you happen to know that my late father had a Montenegrin Albanian blood brother? He was a Muslim Albanian. Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I did not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I mentioned that in my interviews, but did you note in my interviews that my next-door neighbour in Niksic was Mahmut Adzajlic, the uncle of the great Montenegrin hero Mujo Adzajlic who was a Muslim and -- but fought against the Turks?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not noted that in your interviews. I don't have any reason to believe at this time in your life that you harboured ill feelings towards Muslims or toward -- toward Muslims in general or certainly the individual Muslims that you knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that the Montenegrins mostly go to Belgrade to study at university and that they usually study history or law? A little bit of an anecdote now.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm dying to hear it. I'm interested in why you went to Sarajevo, but that's another story, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I'll explain that too. Since Radio Belgrade couldn't be heard in Niksic and Radio Titograd began broadcasting at 12.00, we always listened to Radio Sarajevo, and we saw Bosnia as something very close to us, and instead of going to Belgrade like all the other Montenegrins, I went to Sarajevo because of my love for Sarajevo. How does that sound to you, does it sound plausible?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would -- that's close to my understanding of how it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that in 1960, when I was a 15-year-old boy coming to Sarajevo, that the circumstances and situation in Yugoslavia was very far from any kind of nationalism or disruption of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That year could be the pinnacle, the high point of Yugoslavia as a state that was really quite free from these nationalist divisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, what you said a moment ago, that I was well integrated or what was it, what was the word you used, in Sarajevo, that I felt very good in Sarajevo and despite my Montenegrin identity and entity, I took on the Sarajevo entity and identity as well. So do you accept that where you hail from gives you one identity and your national identity gives you another identity?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know about that general proposition. I think what you're suggesting in general is what I call a hybrid identity, and it's something that actually most of us in one way or another have, a loyalty to a country or a nation and often to a city or locale and sometimes to a family or even a profession simultaneously, and I think the way you described your feelings about Sarajevo and your -- I think you're using in the B/C/S the term "zavicajno," your, let's say, home-base loyalty to Montenegro. That's -- that's exactly as I understood it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But you're not the only one. Some Montenegrin writers, too, saw the fact that I love Montenegro and Montenegro's entity, my opting for the Montenegrin nation. But Montenegro for all Serbs is something that is very respected. They all respect the ethics of Montenegro, that the Serbs are -- highly respect the Montenegro ethics, ethos, not ethnos?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but they tell terrible jokes about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, we all tell jokes like that about all of us. Now, do you know, and I also spoke about this in my interviews, that all my business contacts in Sarajevo were mostly with Muslims? I don't want to enumerate them all, not to waste time. The professor who taught me clinical psychiatry was a Muslim, and I chose him. My internal medicine professor was a Croat, Ivan. My dentist, according to my own choice, is Faruk, a Muslim. My lawyers, once again due to my personal choice, are Ekrem and -- I know the surname but I'll remember his name too. He was also a Muslim, and I think he originated from Kosovo. That my hairdresser is a Muslim, or barber, and that everything I did in Sarajevo was mostly linked to the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I wouldn't really -- I wouldn't quarrel with that, but I think that the time that you got there and the time that you entered into many of these relationships, no one was paying much attention to this identity other than as a basis for kind of casual conversation and personal interest. So it wasn't really a matter of I'm -- and I think this is what you're saying, you didn't deliberately seek out Muslims because they were Muslims for this, but many of the professional people that you engaged with were Muslims or Croats by -- basically by coincidence. Is that what I understand you to be saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you understood me correctly, but the fact remains that those relationships of mine lasted until the outbreak of the war in 1992. Nothing changed. My last haircut was at Meha's [phoen]. He was my barber, the best barber in Sarajevo. And I didn't select him -- I didn't choose him because he was a Muslim but because he was the best, but I didn't not choose him because he was a Muslim. So I want to link up something that you said, that on the 13th of July -- yes. I've been asked to slow down for the benefit of the interpreters. I will. But my point is this: In Sarajevo, there were very prominent professionals among all three ethnic groups, the Serbs, the Muslims, and Croats, and I always looked at the -- their professional capabilities and didn't choose according to religion. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I understand your life at that time, that's true, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And that went right up until the outbreak of the war. Even in March, after - what's it called? - the barricades. Right up until the 6th of April I had the same people and interacted with them. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that it lasted that long for everyone that you were associated with who was of another ethnicity, but I certainly find it plausible that that was the case with some -- some of those folks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to link that up to what you say in your report about the origins of Republika Srpska and that I, on the 13th of July, said, I'll read it out in English: "[In English] At the SDS meeting Karadzic had kind words for the Muslims, 'Our goal is to repair the relations between the nationalities and to establish equality, reciprocity, and civil peace. I believe in the great potentials of the Muslim nation. I believe in its simple humane good.'" This is page 20. [Interpretation] I haven't read it all out, but that's as far as I got, and what I want to -- us to establish now is this: That our relationship -- or, rather, whether our relationship towards the Muslims was political or religious, our relationship towards Islam in general, was it the cause of anything? And in view of the fact that you noticed and recorded those words, do you believe that we really stood by what we said there?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You certainly stood by what you said in the subsequent several months prior to the election when the three national parties, particularly the last few weeks of the election campaign, were holding joint rallies, made appearances together. You made appearances with Mr. Kljujic and Mr. Izetbegovic, worked together to ensure registration of all voters, and in general became a kind of partnered opponents of the Social Democrats and Reformists in the election campaign. So I see that period right up until the election and a little bit beyond it as characterised by these kinds of cooperative sentiments and -- and actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You called them Social Democrats and Reformists very kindly, but we fought against them as Communists for replacing the regime. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the name I guess technically at that point was the Social Democratic Party/League of Communists. So we're, I think, both right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, did you happen to note at the founding Assembly of the Serbian Democratic Party, and I see that you saw 3.000 people present, did you happen to notice the programme and platform of the Serbian Democratic Party, and, if so, did anything in that programme attract your attention?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe I summarised a few points anyway in the paper, but frankly, it's been a while since I looked at it. If you are prepared to refresh my memory or something I'd be -- be happy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well I hope we'll be able to call up on e-court the party programme, but let me ask you this: Do you remember the speech I delivered at the founding Assembly?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally, yes, but I don't remember specific words or passages.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have 1390 called up, please, which is the programme of the Serb Democratic Party at the founding session on the 12th of July, 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm sure you noticed that I didn't wish to be the party president and that I offered the position to everybody else. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm sure you also noted that I proposed that there be a national wing and a social democratic wing?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I referred to that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you speak Serbian -- well, perhaps the Prosecution has the translation of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In fact, this appears on the Prosecution's 65 ter list as 00928, and there is a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Shall we wait for the translation then. 00928. May we have that called up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm going to read it out in Serbian, and we see the English on the screen. "Programme of the Serbian Democratic Party of BH. "In the process of revitalisation of political life in -- of Serbian people in BH in the spirit of liberty-oriented traditions, the Serbian Democratic Party of Bosnia and Herzegovina finds its activities on the following humanistic and civilised principles and objectives. "1" --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we zoom in, please thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "Democracy that rests on the abolishment of the monopoly of one political party. "2. Peace and co-operation among people as the prerequisite of development and social progress. "3. Freedom and rights to humans and citizens as supreme values. "4. Legitimate authority and rule of law. "5. Equality as the basis of cohabitation. "6. A democratic Yugoslavia as a modern federal state. "7. International relations -- internationality relations founded on mutual respect and tolerance. "8. The establishment of equal, fair, and civilised dialogue of legitimately elected representatives of all peoples and citizens. "9. Bosnia and Herzegovina as a republic with equal rights within a modern federal state. "10. Kosovo and Metohija within the state of Serbia with autonomy of the Western European type. "11. Co-operation with the Serbian Orthodox church and its involvement in the life of the Serbian people on an equal basis." Now, I don't have 12 there in the Serbian, but anyway. "Return to cultural, historical and national heritage alienated from" -- Do you want me to read it all? I don't think there's any need for me to go through them all, all these points. We have the programme before us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You could have stopped a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Let's look at number 20; that's an important point. "20. The development of rural areas and agriculture by abolishing the land maximum and taxes and to have agrarian policy to protect the farmers from the vagaries of agriculture," et cetera. Was this a programme a correct programme and acceptable to one and all?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Much of it was. I think there are a few points here that provided an entry point into the debates that took place during the pre-election campaign and on which there were some pronounced differences, and I would -- if I could go back to the first page, perhaps. There is -- number 6, the "Democratic Yugoslavia as a modern federal state." And number 9, "Bosnia and Herzegovina as a republic with equal rights want modern federal state," would become a source of contention. Not so much for what they said, but for how they were interpreted by you and other party leaders in terms of some of the constitutional debates that we talked about yesterday. I think the -- the rest of this -- certainly point 10 is really a statement of -- almost advocates returning to Kosovo and Metohija the autonomy that it had lost, that had been taken from it by Milosevic in 1989, and so I think on that point you would have found -- you did find wide agreement with the other parties. Now, without looking at all the rest of them, I think I've identified two, anyway, that would become the source of contention in the course of the election campaign. I think pretty much everything else is -- was widely accepted and hailed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall then we announced that we would be forming the SDS on the 26th of March, 1990? Izetbegovic wrote that he not even talk to any of the parties that were in favour of the dismantling of Yugoslavia. Actually, the SDA party. It was their first proclamation in which they announced the setting up of their party.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I don't have a specific recollection of that statement. It would certainly be the case that the SDA, the Muslim party, in its first platform expressed support for Bosnia-Herzegovina as a unified republic within Yugoslavia and that it should be within Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You noticed, then, confirmed that Mr. Izetbegovic, with the other Muslim leaders, actually attended this first founding Assembly, welcomed it, and he said, "What have you been waiting for? We are waiting for an authentic Serbian party." Is that not the case?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think his words were more, "We have been waiting for you."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's right. Do you recall when somebody from the audience asked him, "What kind of a Yugoslavia are you in favour of?" And he replied, "I'm in favour of a reasonable federation."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Words to that effect I do recall, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember how I explained why Krajisnik was the president, the speaker of the Assembly, and why he was often in -- on negotiating teams? In addition to his obvious ability, I also said that it was Izetbegovic's wish for Krajisnik to be on those teams because they understood each other well.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have a specific recollection of that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, but I wish to point out this: When I said -- when we said that a democratic Yugoslavia is regulated as a modern democratic state, was this something what -- that Izetbegovic wanted? He wanted a reasonable federation. Was it a step towards that reasonable federation that he wanted, that we had made to accommodate his wish?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- well, I think this enters into the question of what was meant by "federation" and what was meant by "confederation." I think your question, though, is a little bit different in that you're suggesting, I take it, that Izetbegovic supported Mr. Krajisnik's participation because he liked his approach to a modern Yugoslavia. Is that what you are suggesting?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I want to say that we took into account what sat well with the Muslim side. So I asked the Muslim side what their opinion would be if Milan Trbojevic or Krajisnik were to become speaker of the Assembly, because we wanted to avoid any misunderstandings. That is why I chose this formulation, a modern federal state in order for [indiscernible] to be affected with the view that Izetbegovic held. Do you agree that I managed to do that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think there are two quite separate topics here. One is the selection of the president of the Presidency, the president of the Assembly, and the president of the government, which was done in accord with the inter-party agreements after the elections. And I think we're still talking about the compatibility of the approaches to Yugoslavia which characterised this period right around the founding of the parties but quickly diverged into two quite different views of what it meant to be a modern federal state.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I wasn't clear enough. I myself was not in favour of Yugoslavia's remaining the way it was, so the term I used, "modern federation," is something that I wanted actually to use in order to be as close as possible to the formulation which Izetbegovic used, which was a "reasonable federation." Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the modern -- the formulation of the modern preceded what -- what Izetbegovic said. I -- I do not know what consultations you may have had with him prior to the adoption of the platform, but the platform was adopted at the founding Assembly on -- in July, and at that same meeting, I believe, is when he made that statement. The issues subsequently centred around statements during the campaign where clearly there was a difference of views on what Yugoslavia should be and what it should be called, as well as what it -- what any changes in it should amount to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you note anywhere in my interviews that Izetbegovic and I myself were neighbours and that we used to see each other before either his or my party were set up, and even before this founding Assembly was held I knew what views he held?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fine. I wasn't aware of -- I don't know how much contact you had with him, but I certainly find that plausible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be tendered into evidence and can we call up P929, please, the OTP's document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 928 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D254, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see document 929 of the OTP. That is my speech at this founding Assembly. First of all, we should like to see the first page, and then if we could move on to page 4, please. We do not have to devote any time to the entire speech. We just have to focus on the relevant segments of it. 929. Prosecution exhibit. 65 ter -- 65 ter 00929. The Serbian version is there. Now we need the English one. Yes. This is the inaugural speech of the founding Assembly. Can we now look at page 4. Can we see page 4, please. Actually, in the English version it is page 3, and it is all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at this penultimate paragraph which starts with "Co-existence."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you scroll up the Serbian version a bit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "Co-existence has also created some permanent values which the Serbian Democratic Party will nurture and develop. In that sense, the party shall be open to co-operation" - can we please go to the next page in the Serbian version - "with all democratic organisations in the republic and the country. We can cannot and shall not co-operate with parties which have even the slightest trace of anti-Serbianism, anti-Yugoslavism, anti-Semitism, and anti-democracy in their programme or dealings. "The name the party is its most complete and its most correct legitimacy. It is the party of the Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina. It is a democratic party which will work in the interests of the Serbian people and citizens and thereby also in the interests of all peoples and citizens in our region." Did you notice or did you know, were you aware, of this speech of mine?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that Izetbegovic's standpoint voiced on the 26th of March to the effect that he would not even talk to parties that were in favour of dismantling Yugoslavia and his statement that he was in favour of a modern federation, and that this part of my speech, of my programme, were good foundations for a future coalition of these two national parties?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I indicated earlier, I'm not aware of that specific statement from 26th of March. I am aware that he embraced something in the language that was close to -- I think it was a -- a modern state or a modern -- it could have been modern federation. It -- I've never been able to figure out exactly who you had in mind with that phrase that you would not -- and would not co-operate with parties who have the slightest bit of anti-Serbian, anti-Yugoslav, anti-Semitic and anti-democratic inclinations. That seemed to me a wide barn door which could be interpreted by just about anybody to encompass all sorts of parties that you planned not to co-operate with. It's very open. But I think with the exception of that statement which leaves me a bit puzzled, this was indeed a sound basis for co-operation with the SDA as a partner party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see page 3, paragraph 2 in the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And until that is called up, can I remind you that we already had the Croatian Party of Rights in Zagreb, in Croatia, which inherited the traditions of the Party of Rights from the Ustasha times, which actually engender the Ustashas. Actually, it was the Croatian Party of Rights that had engendered the Ustasha movement prior to the Second World War, a fascist movement which actually created the Independent State of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's comment by Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I've been wondering who's giving evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall, do you agree that the Croatian Party of Rights had set up the Ustasha movement which was at the helm of the independent State of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the Croatian Party of Rights was restored and that its work was revived in the 1990s, in the early 1990s, in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a political group that was formed called the Croatian Party of Rights that claimed the heritage of the earlier Croatian Party of Rights. I don't know that it -- we could say it was revived. It was formed, I would think, anew and claimed those -- that tradition.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that that Croatian Party of Rights again restored the demands for the -- for the restoration of the Independent State of Croatia, which would include Boka Kotorska, Srijem and other territories that it previously included?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- to be that specific, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But they published this map, and they said they were reviving the work of the Croatian Party of Rights upon the same programme. Do you agree that the basis for the Croatian Party of Rights is Ante Starcevic's ideology?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In part, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the new, just like the old, Croatian Party of Rights was markedly anti-Serbian, anti-Yugoslavian, and anti-Semitic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the Ustashas were anti-Yugoslav, anti-Serbian, and anti-Semitic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You recall you confirmed that we even had certain doubts in respect of President Tudjman when he said that he was happy, that he was fortunate that his wife was neither Serbian nor Jewish?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We confirmed that statement, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the light of that, does this position that we will not co-operate with anti-Serbian, anti-democratic, anti-Yugoslav, anti-Semitic parties, does it now seem justified to you in that speech which we saw?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if it's justified or not. I simply said I really don't know what you meant by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But is it clear now when I point out the fact to you that there existed an even more extreme and even more rightist party than the Croatian Democratic Union was, and that we could expect that even more right-wing parties would be formed, and that we had the right to say with whom we would not be co-operating because we had before our eyes the existing examples, and the HDZ was partly an a party of that ilk?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I read it, it looked to me like it opened the door for you to say you would not co-operate with just about anybody that you chose not to co-operate with. It was a wide-open designation, and you reserved the right to label any group that you found to be so with one of those labels.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you co-operate -- would you have co-operated with a party of anti-Serbian, anti-Yugoslav, anti-Semitic, anti-democratic orientation? Or any such exclusivist orientation, would you have co-operated, in our shoes, with them?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I -- I think you -- when I first read this, I thought you were referring to the League of Communists with your anti-democratic statement. I would have no trouble co-operating with the League of Communists if I had been in your situation at that time. But again, I don't know who you meant here, and it seemed to me to leave the door wide open. So I really couldn't give you a meaningful answer to that question without delving into exactly who you considered anti-Serb, anti-democratic, anti-Yugoslav, or anti-Semitic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I read out for you the second paragraph on page 3. "The basic -- the basic aim of the party's full and unconditional civil, national, cultural, religious, and economic equality of the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina. We cannot have leading and auxiliary peoples, first-rate and second-rate citizens, constituent and unconstituent elements." It is the second page in the English version. And we shall see what Mr. Zulfikarpasic had to say about this, about whom you know quite a few things. But let us conclude. Is this a decent and acceptable programme and speech at the founding Assembly of this party?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would only be troubled by the degree to which you suggested that the Serb Nation is such an integrated, delineated, highly identifiable group, and furthermore, by the degree to which you saw the previous couple of decades as injuring, depleting the welfare of the Serb people that you postulated as existing. That seemed to me to open the door to recriminations and blame pointing that would not be constructive in the course of a political party's life. That observation is -- really goes to the kind of, let's say, concept that you had at that point already of an integral Serbian people and set out about assessing its welfare based on standards that you applied from your own experience and -- and views. I find the list of objectives of the party to be, again, I have not read through all of them, but those that I have seen here look to me to be laudable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And was the Serbian people in Yugoslavia, whatever it was called, was it integrated into a single state, that it was already an achievement, it was something that had already been achieved? It was not something that I had to accomplish in 1990.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what's the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that I was in favour of integrating the entire Serbian nation. Was the entire Serbian nation integrated in Yugoslavia in 1918 when it entered Yugoslavia as a unitary kingdom?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think it's -- that those who identify themselves as Serbs have ever been as integrated, distinct and compact as you suggest they were at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I don't understand what you want to say. What I want to say is this: In 1918, all Serbs, Croats, Muslims, Slovenes lived in one state through integration, integration with themselves and with other peoples; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were a good number of Croats living outside of the Trianon kingdom. There were -- or the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes. There were many Muslims living outside that polity, Slovenes in Austria and Italy. Were they -- were the bulk of those people, the most of those who identified themselves as such residents of the new Yugoslav state or the Kingdom of Croats, Slovenes -- Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, yes, they were, but I wouldn't call them integrated in the sense that they didn't live anywhere else or that they were all compactly joined together in a single polity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, the facts are different to what we're saying. It was a united country that was later divided into banovinas; right? But it remained a unitary state until 1945 or, rather, 1941; it was a unitary monarchy.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, maybe it's quarreling with the term, but I think that very soon as the kingdom -- in the history of the kingdom, the rejection of much of the Croatian political elite of the form that the state had taken would bring that into question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to tender this document into evidence. First of all the programme, the platform; and second, my inaugural speech at the SDS party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we have already admitted the programme and then we'll admit this speech, which is of three pages, I take it. Yes. We'll admit it. Give the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D255, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May we back to page number 4 in Serbian to show you that there was co-operation with the Communists and that there was no revanchism. If you omitted to see that, I just wanted to point that out to you. There was no revanchism. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I agree there was no expression of revanchism here. I didn't suggest there was. I simply said that in terms of the party, the League of Communists, that it may have been among those that would have been referred to in parties that you had no intention of co-operating with. But I agree with your statement. There was an open expression by you here of the openness of the SDS to those members of the League of Communists or people who had been members of the League of Communists to join the SDS if they subscribed to its programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But just to see that we didn't dispute their right to have their party, and if we look at this paragraph there won't be any revanchism or anti-communism. We don't question anybody's right to political life, to the electoral campaign and participation in the government. Furthermore, the party will be open to all democratically minded Communists, Socialists, and other parties who accept the programme of the Serbian Democratic Party, et cetera, et cetera. So we tried to deal with the ideological differences and even them out.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we're finished with that document now. Thank you. It can be removed from the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Donia, do you agree that the pre-electoral campaign evolved in a tolerant atmosphere for the most part, without any excesses or incidents or impediments?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that the only thing that we at the time demanded was a different designing, if I can use the term, of the municipalities and the municipal communities?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That certainly is not the only thing that you were demanding. I think it was part of -- it played a role in the electoral campaign and was certainly a part of the general critique of the Communist era that was part of the electoral campaign targeted specifically against the League of Communists party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, did you happen to note a moment ago in the programme that we were in favour of abolishing the maximum land holding and that that existed in Communist Yugoslavia, the land holding maximum which meant that a household could not have more than ten hectares of land?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did note the provision in the platform, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you agree that that was most detrimental to the Serbs because they were mostly an agricultural people in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you agree that it was mostly the Serbs who lived, mostly I say, in the rural areas, whereas the Croats and Muslims, especially the Muslims, lived in urban areas, in the towns?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. We can prove that very easily. But do you agree that the new power and authority in all the republics abolished this communist restriction of land holdings to ten hectares and that after that everybody could have as much land as they wanted?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about all the republics, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sure you remember and know that we were victorious at the elections. We beat all the three national parties, the former Communists, rallied in the Reformists and Socialists, and we managed to realise our coalition platform; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's accurate to say that the three national parties won the election and won it at all levels and in most municipalities. The former Communists in the form of the Social Democratic Party and the Reformists did well in certain areas and prevailed, for example, in the municipality of Tuzla and in -- they did well in Novi Grad, the municipality of Sarajevo. The -- so, yes, there was a victory. Yes, it was convincing, but it wasn't universal. The term that I believe you preferred to use at the time was not coalition platform but, rather, a partnership of three parties, and that partnership rested largely on respecting the inter-party agreements that had been reached verbally during the campaign period, and then there were some actual agreement in writing that inter-party agreements being an agreement to divide offices in each municipality and at the republic level according to the percentage of votes that each of the national parties received. Those inter-party agreements completely excluded the 20 to 25 per cent of those elected in the election of 1990 who were a part of what was called the opposition. So they were both distributive and exclusionary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the Chamber is minded to take a break earlier than usual, if it is convenient. We'll break now. Twenty-five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, I'm not going to ask you whether you vote for the democrats or republicans, but I see that you feel sorry for our left wingers, for us not including them in executive power. Now, do you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic repeat his question, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, did you note that? Could you repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I said that I see you feel sorry for our left wingers, for not -- for us not including them in executive power, but I'm sure you'll agree that the elections are there to change the powers?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, some elections change power and some keep it the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you what you meant when you said that we excluded the left-wing parties. Do you hold that against us?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I referred to the inter-party agreements and pointed out that the inter-party agreements as they were struck and carried out were exclusionary in that they excluded from power the Social Democratic Party, League of Communists, and the Reformists and other small parties that won a few seats here and there and that that was -- well, it meant that there was a -- an opposition which became known as the left opposition but, in fact, included parties that were of quite different orientations. The Reformists really were not a leftist party as much as they were a Reformist Party. So the agreements did, in fact, mean that the three national parties together monopolised control of power at the republic level, the level of the city of Sarajevo, and in almost all municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But you're not disputing the fact that these parties gained their place in legislation and all the boards, the Municipal Boards. I mean, the opposition parties; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe they were excluded from the municipal executive organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: From all the executive organs at the level of the republic and at the level of the municipalities, because they lost power. But they did take part in legislative power; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In those -- in those areas where they had representatives in the Municipal Assemblies, yes, they did. And note the one exception of Tuzla and, I believe, originally -- was it Vares where they actually did very well also, and I think briefly had a role in the executive of Vares municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now to move on -- well, before we move on I'd like to go back to your origins of Republika Srpska, page 9, where you say that: "The new constitution according to Serbia -- [In English] New constitution gave additional powers to the president of the republic, including powers -- power to command armed forces in peace and war." [Interpretation] [No interpretation]. "[In English] It assured the centralisation of the Serbian Republic by eliminating the autonomy formerly enjoyed by Kosovo and Vojvodina." [Interpretation] Do you agree that Vojvodina and Kosovo, up until 1974, had one type of autonomy?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were named autonomous. One was an autonomous province, one was an autonomous region, and, yes, they enjoyed some degree of autonomy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that with the 1974 constitution they were given a further degree of autonomy, right up to the fact that they were able to control Serbia and their legislative power?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They weren't able to control Serbia, but they were given added autonomy by the 1974 constitution. As we indicated yesterday, they acquired many of the characteristics of a republic in the -- in federal organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that Serbia was not able to enact certain laws until it had the agreement of the Assemblies of Vojvodina and Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up until their -- either the -- as in the case of the Assembly of Kosovo, it was abolished, or in the case of Vojvodina, up until the period of the new constitution, that is 1989, I believe, 1990, that was indeed the case, yes. I just want to be clear about the time-frame we're talking about, from 1974 to 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Now, when in 1989 and 1990 this situation was changed with the constitution, was autonomy abolished or just part of the added rights that they gained under the 1974 constitution? Were just those abolished?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main components of autonomy were abolished but not all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And would you agree that even given that situation, that Vojvodina and Kosovo had more autonomy than they had before 1974?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was there less autonomy they had up until 1974 then -- before 1974.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I understand the question, and I have the impression that, yes, they did have less, but if you were, you know, to ask me in what way and specifically what, I couldn't tell you. So I think my best answer would be I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if I tell you that the aim and intentions achieved with the 1990 constitution was that Serbia could enact laws throughout its territory, laws relating to the whole of its territory, that that was the pivotal point of that constitutional amendment and not the abolishment of autonomy, would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would say that the primary purpose and consequence of the constitution of 1990 was centralisation of Serbia, and that included dramatically reducing the autonomy that the two areas had enjoyed from 1974 to 1990. I think its primary purpose was to create a more centralised governance, which is in accord with what you just proposed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But it's not all the same is it, Mr. Donia, I'm sure you will agree, whether autonomy was abolished or whether what was abolished was the exaggerated rights of the provinces to control the legislature and legislative activities of Serbia. And do you think, for example, that in New Hampshire, if New Hampshire were to make a decision to -- could it stop the functioning of Congress, for example, if it took it into its head to do that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Texas, maybe, but I think the point of this is that the centralisation inherently means reducing autonomy of those parts of the state that the previously enjoyed it. That would be the case anywhere. And you have stepped into the dispute. That is, there are residents of Kosovo and Metohija, at least the Albanian residents of Kosovo would argue that these were rights that they were entitled to and were now being denied to them in 1990, and Serbs would say the opposite. It's contested.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I just want to say that we don't see eye to eye there, that autonomy was abolished. It was reduced with respect to what was accorded in 1974, but what I'm saying is that even after that, the provinces had more autonomy than they had prior to 1974. But if you don't agree with that, we'll go on to prove and show that in due course. Do you agree -- well, you said that no agreement had been signed, but do you agree that the criteria had been adopted for the distribution of power and authority among those three parties?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you also agree that a principle was established according to the number of votes or seats in parliament, municipal and others, that that was the numerical criterion that was to be respected?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is the case, but the -- my understanding of the inter-party agreement was that certain percentages were awarded that were approximations of the votes received or the delegates won by each party. So the leading party, the first party, got, I believe, the president of the Assembly, the Municipal Assembly, or in the case of the republican government, the president of the Presidency, and so on. There was a hierarchy created among the three parties which pertained -- which was based on the number of delegates elected from -- in each municipality and at the republic level.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May we now have on e-court 1D93 -- 1392, 1392, please. Just to have a quick glance at those criteria which were binding upon us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, do you remember that at lower levels down the chain, if the chief of a security station was from one party, then the police commander would be from another party?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: First to this document, yes, this is indeed the percentages agreement that the three parties reached. I believe this document was dated December, after the elections were complete, but was clearly the basis or the result of earlier discussions and agreements. I became aware of this document, I believe, after I had prepared the origins of RS report, but have been aware of it for some time since then. The key question, in fact, was the issue of who got the chief of police position and who got the chief of the police station job, and then there was a third position, I believe it was head of traffic police or something like that, that entered into the formula. And, in fact, while that was the most important set of offices to be divvied up according to the agreement, it, in fact, was invoked in a wide variety of other positions in the government and in the -- the government of the republic and in the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May I read something to you. Well, the party that won 5 per cent gets a vice-presidency position, which is on a volunteer basis, not paid. And from 5 to 10 per cent --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour. Before Dr. Karadzic begins to read from the document, it's 65 ter number 18514, I'm informed, and the translation of the document should be available within about seven seconds, I hope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. That would be better. I had counted upon Mr. Donia understanding Serbian, so that's why I did that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It might be about 30 seconds. I may have underestimated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's coming.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, indeed it is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we just have the page in English first, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So from 5 to 10 per cent, one vice-presidential volunteer position, and one position in the executive government; right? Then from 15 to 20 per cent -- other, rather, from 11 per cent to 20 per cent there's a vice-presidential place, a professional, and one department. From 21 to 32 per cent, one vice-presidential place to be filled by a professional in two departments. From 33 per cent to 50 per cent the stronger side can choose first, either to be president of a municipality or president of the other sector. That's the municipal government; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I do hope you'll go on and read: "Napomena lijeve stranke se ne uzimaju u obzir."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, we'd had enough of them for 45 years, in actual fact. Do you agree that we had enough of the left-wing parties by that time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Excuse me, what Dr. Donia said was not translated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And unfortunately I checked it myself, but there seems to be no English translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Actually, my colleague has to -- I think they know what to do, Your Honours. Something technical involving re-releasing the document so that my colleague Mr. Reid can attach the translation to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Note: The left-wing parties are not taken into account is what it says.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In fact, as I've seen how fast these two are working, my respect for them has risen commensurately.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Donia said that the note at the bottom says that the left-wing parties are not taken into consideration, and my answer to him was that we had them for all of 45 years and that we'd had enough of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you agree that 45 years of a leftist monopoly was quite enough?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You sound like you're still bitter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, no. I was a dissident, but the fact remains that the people decided to elect another government. Do you agree? A different government.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the electorate voted for the three national parties, first and foremost; but it was the decision of the three national parties working together to exclude the League of Communists and other parties that were -- made up the left opposition, which was in contradiction to what you had stated at the founding Assembly of the SDS, that the members of the League of Communists were free to participate in the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. They all could participate in the government, but our standpoint was that there would be no revanchism, that there would be no lastration [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you agree that this is there where the -- where two parties had won at the elections and came to power? And on the next page we have three parties sharing the power. So the first page we had power sharing by two parties in West Herzegovina. There were the Muslims and the Croats. There were no Serbs there. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, okay. So just to clarify, one page - I'm not sure which one - addresses a situation in which three parties, all three national parties, won certain numbers of votes, and the other is if only two parties competed essentially and won votes in a municipality. Is that -- I think that's what I'm seeing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That is right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the next page in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: These are also mixed communities with all the three ethnic communities participating, and all the three parties made it to the municipal parliament.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm afraid that we don't have the translation of the second page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I move to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, until that is done, do you agree that this was an agreement struck by the parties who had won over 80 per cent of the seats in the respective government bodies?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think about 80 per cent is right. I'm not too sure it quite got to 80 per cent, but in some municipalities it got to more and in some nowhere near that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But at the republican level it was approximately 80 per cent; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that immediately following the elections I proposed that in order to ease political tensions that an expert government rather than a party government be formed? Government of experts.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And as, you know, this was not accepted.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the Serbian Democratic Party adhered to that position and delegated to the government at the central level experts except for one party person. So those people were not, with the exception of Mr. Ostojic, party people. Let me remind you. Mr. Ostojic was a member of the party and the president of the Executive Board, and the other members of the cabinet were not members of the Serbian Democratic Party. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall. I know there were 18 ministers appointed altogether, and something like a third of them were appointed by the SDS. I don't remember how many were party members.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me try to jog your memory. There were 18 ministers, but there were also deputy ministers in all 36 members of the government, because the deputy minister is also a member of the government; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It -- the term "government" being the equivalent of what in the United States is the cabinet or in European systems is the council of ministers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Do you remember that where the minister was a Serb -- or, rather, from the SDS, the deputy minister was either from the HDZ or the SDA and vice versa?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that the vice-premier on behalf of the SDS was Dr. Miodrag Simovic, who was not a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Dr. Simovic being a constitutional lawyer, I believe, at that time and today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the previous regime he had been persecuted, and he was on the slate of the Serbian Democratic Party. Do you remember that the minister of justice was Ranko Pejic, who had also been a minister in the previous regime and who had also been persecuted?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about any prosecution or persecution of either Dr. Simovic or Mr. Pejic. I just know that they were in the positions that you indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I give you a summary. Miodrag Simovic was the vice-premier, Momcilo Pejic was in the finance department. Perhaps you have a list. Perhaps the OTP has a list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have a list, but with respect, I would suggest that it's inappropriate for Dr. Karadzic to be delivering a summary. It would -- if he has something to ask of Dr. Donia in respect of these individuals, it would best be in the form of a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Agreed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I thought that would be more expeditious.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that Momcilo Pejic was the finance minister and he was not a member of the Serbian Democratic Party?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that he was appointed Finance Minister. I don't know what his relationship to the democratic -- Serb Democratic Party was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that both Pejics, Momcilo Pejic and Ranko Pejic, had been ministers in the preceding period, in the Communist period?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that the deputy minister of health was Dr. Tatjana Starovic-Medan and that she was not a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recall that she was deputy minister of health, but again I don't know anything of her relationship to the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that Professor Branko Djeric was a minister for development, I believe. He was not a member of the SDS, but he was a member of the political council as a nonparty member, nonparty person.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm familiar with Professor Djeric's biography later on in the war. He was, I believe, prime minister of the government of the RS, but I don't know of his relationship to the SDS at the time that he assumed this ministerial position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that the agriculture minister was Professor Milivoje Nadazdin, who also was not a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I tell you that they all were eminent experts in their professions and were not members of the SDS, this is something that you will not challenge. I mean, you have no information to the contrary.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no information about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that leading the slate of the Serbian Democratic Party in the Sarajevo electoral district was the president of the cultural society Prosveta, Professor Maksimovic, who at that moment was not a member of the SDS and was ipso facto a nonparty person?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You seem to be qualifying that. I remember Professor Maksimovic as an SDS member from very early on, and perhaps he was not at that moment, but I think he became a member very soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You are right. Do you remember that Milan Trbojevic was among the first six and that he never actually became a member of the SDS and he was a deputy to parliament?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that in the Banja Luka electoral district the -- leading the slate was Vojo Kupresanin, who was the head and founder of a small party, the Homeland Front, which joined up with for the needs of election, for the purpose of the election?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do I remember he led the slate? I do remember that, and I know of the Homeland Front. I know that the Homeland Front was active in the Banja Luka area. I was not aware that he was the head and founder of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that Mr. Vitomir Zepinic was the deputy minister of the interior and that was never a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you accept that none of the chiefs of security services centres -- no. Let me begin this way: Do you know what security service centres were in contrast to station -- public security stations?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Security stations exist in every municipality, whereas centres are at the level of a number of municipalities; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I have no reason to doubt that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you -- you did properly notice that there was quite a struggle around those positions. Did you notice that there were many contenders for those positions in Banja Luka and there --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the interpreter is unable to follow Mr. Karadzic. Could he please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the interpreters were not able to follow you, so could you slow down and then repeat what you just said.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So in Banja Luka there were two streams contending to appoint two honourable people, Jevto Jankovic was a judge and a member of the party, and Stojan Zupljanin was not a member of the party but he had experience as a policeman. Do you remember that I, and this was published, with Zepinic, actually decided that the person with the police experience should be appointed to that position?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I tell you now that in all the centres of security services none of the chiefs of security service centres on the list on the slate of the Serbian Democratic Party in both republic and state security departments were members of the SDS? Would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not without further evidence of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: A correction. Simo Drljaca, in Prijedor, was a member of the party, but do you know that Stojan Zupljanin was not a member of the party?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, two points. This has gone on for some long time now, and I'm actually completely at a loss as to what the relevance of this line of questioning might be. And the second is about the formulation, in fact, of these questions, Your Honour. I've risen a couple of times on the comment and evidence-giving by Dr. Karadzic, and it seems to me that every single one of these successive questions is formulated with a statement of evidence by the accused before he gets to the actual question, and I'm wondering how much longer this should go on for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the Chamber would like to remind you that only Dr. Donia's answers are evidence. Any comment, statement, or observation by yourself at this point is not evidence. So we would like to remind you of what we said previously: "The Chamber is concerned that you are not making more effective use of your time for your cross-examination. The Chamber is therefore contemplating setting time limits on your cross-examination of each witness which we will determine on a witness-by-witness basis and which you will be required to comply with unless you can show good cause why additional time is necessary. Should you not demonstrate during your cross-examination that you are seriously taking our advice, the Chamber will begin to impose such a time limit." So bear that in mind, and following the advice you take from your legal advisors as well as the Bench, conduct your cross-examination efficiently. We'll see.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Well, possibly paradoxically, I might be losing time in my attempt to gain time and avoid entering into greater investigation with Mr. Donia or establishing the truth with Mr. Donia. So maybe that's the mistake I have been making, which is not my intention, of course. But this line of questioning is very important for me, because it is my case that the Serbian Democratic Party won power but did not seize it but handed it over to the experts. And that's a very important point, a landmark for many things from the pre-trial brief, and later on we'll see why.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Donia, do you agree that in the executive power and authority the Serb Democratic Party did not appoint party cadres, predominantly party cadres, but cadres that it found in the various services, who were already there?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If by "party cadres" you mean party members, I think in the main that was the case for the -- for the cabinet, for the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the main.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you agree that in the police force and in the top positions we did not bring in anybody who was not already, for example, in the police force and that those people weren't party members, except in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, would I not agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you give us the name of a high-ranking police officer who was a party member?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just simply can't accept the proposition that was the -- the way that you put it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about Vitomir Zepinic as deputy minister, the highest Serb post in the Ministry of the Interior. Was he ever a member of the party? Let's take him as an example.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was not the -- oh, the highest Serb post in the Ministry of the Interior. To my knowledge, he was never a member of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And if I tell you that he wasn't -- that Mico Stanisic at that time was not either, or any of the chiefs of the security services, would you agree with me there, or do you have proof and evidence that that was not the case?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about Mico Stanisic. I know that he was shortly thereafter a party member, but I don't know about the time that you're speaking of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And did you happen to notice that the leadership of the party was subjected to serious criticism for having given over power and authority to the experts rather than party members?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you agree that the Serbian Democratic Party won the post of president of the Assembly. The SDA had the post of president of the Presidency and the HDZ the post of prime minister.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it came out. I don't know that the -- you could say that the SDS won the post of president of the Assembly.
