That was a product of the inter-party agreements, and the parties under the inter-party agreement, the national parties, acquired the right to designate those three positions because of the percentage of -- of votes that had -- that they'd won at the republic level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you agree that we first of all divided up the posts and then saw who the people were to fill those posts.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That -- I think that's in the main the case. It certainly is the case with the three positions you just named at the republic level and also at the level of the city of Sarajevo. I'm sure it was the case at many municipalities as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you agree that the Ministry of the Interior -- well, that the minister post went to the SDA and the minister of defence post went to the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those two national parties did indeed designate the people for those two positions, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the Serbian Democratic Party did not ask for any of those positions but instead asked for the Ministry of Agriculture and the Ministry of Finance?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Professor Koljevic, in his diary and account of that particular time notes that you had decided not to seek those two positions, that is, the Ministry of the Interior, Ministry of Defence, because the JNA was the dominant military force in the area, so you thought it was -- there was no point in seeking those positions because they were of much less consequence because of the JNA's presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But do you agree that the Croats were very sensitive to the fact of who was going to be minister of defence in view of the presence of the JNA and that we made a concession in that regard, and that we agreed that the minister of defence should be a Croat?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of what negotiations may have led to those designations. I could only say, on the basis of Professor Koljevic's observation, that you didn't regard those two ministries as -- as important to -- for the SDS to seek.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that the reconstitution of the Assembly in his speech, Mr. Izetbegovic's, in mid-January, still remained in favour of the preservation of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that it was a surprise to one and all when, on the 31st of January, Mr. Izetbegovic launched the initiative to adopt the declaration on sovereignty for Bosnia-Herzegovina? We're now speaking about 1991; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: January 1991. No, I don't think it was a surprise to one and all. I would certainly agree that he was the instrumental person in launching that initiative and that the -- basically the leadership of the SDA and most of the HDZ backed that initiative.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the SDS was against that and that in February Mr. Izetbegovic spoke at the Assembly, and we mentioned that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- a number of SDS delegates in the Assembly spoke against the proposal for the declaration of sovereignty once it had been offered in the course of the discussion in, I think -- on the 27th of February, yes. You spoke, I believe, also at that Assembly for -- I think for the first time in the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You confirm that Mr. Avdo Campara, the secretary of the Assembly, on the occasion confirmed that we had the right to send the issue up to the council for the realisation of national equality, and that it was on that basis that any further adoption of that declaration was deferred?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was -- we can see a specific ruling. We were looking at the session yesterday, and he ruled on constitutional grounds that the application of more than 20 delegates to the Assembly would trigger the referral of the proposed legislation to that body, and that until such time as a decision was reached by that body, the measure could not be voted upon. It could be discussed but not voted upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let's go back a bit. Do you remember that on the 7th of January, 1991, in Sarajevo, the resolution of the Muslim intellectuals was made public, calling for a sovereign Bosnia. It was published on the 8th of January, broadcast in the media.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, you asked me yesterday if I would take advantage of the opportunity to review the transcript of that session that we've just been talking about. I wonder if I could respond to that inquiry maybe at this point, because we have just -- just been talking about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know if it's available to bring up again, the -- the transcript of the session of the 27th of February.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it Exhibit P969?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In fact, Your Honours, the whole session is -- the transcript of the whole session of the 27th of February is 65 ter 06291.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for that, I want to ask you: Do you know about this declaration, the resolution of the Muslim intellectuals of the 8th of January?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- yes. It's a long time since I've looked at it. I don't recall much of what it said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you remember that the Presidency of the SFRY, on the 9th of January, issued an order on the dissolution of all irregular armed forces and the surrender of weapons introduced in the country illegally, and that this task was to be carried out by the 19th of January, whereas Croatia asked for an extension of the dead-line by 48 hours?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We can now move on to the 27th of February.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The page on which this occurs is -- in the internal pagination is, I believe, 27/1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm only being amazed by your memory, Doctor. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The -- if Dr. Donia is referring to the page that was displayed yesterday, that's e-court page 101 of this document, and this document is not translated yet, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. The -- I was hoping we might go back to page -- you see the 6. Just back one page to the very bottom of page 5, because I think this passage will add meaningful context to the statement that Mr. Izetbegovic name -- made. Let's see. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you going to read it out or --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is your language, sir. Starting with [Interpretation] "But let me continue," beginning with that. [In English] This --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I see that: "But I'll continue to seek for a solution which, as I said, will fulfil both conditions. In my opinion there are two minimum conditions to be filled. First, the -- a sovereign democratic Bosnia as a whole, and the second important point is" -- may I have the next page, please. "A sovereign integral and democratic Bosnia, and a peaceful road to that. So not through a civil war and dead bodies. The route to that Bosnia should be sought and verified, and we should launch a quest for that road and use every opportunity to advance in that direction. Those two -- but those two conditions which I mentioned here, a sovereign and integral Bosnia-Herzegovina and a peaceful road to it, do not have the same value. Because of a sovereign Bosnia, I would give up peace, but for peace in Bosnia I would not give up a sovereign Bosnia. (Applause). Similarly, because this is contentious and the subject of polemics in the scale of values of Bosna Yugoslavia as a ratio, if I had to choose, BiH would come first and then Yugoslavia. That's how it stands for me. (Applause)." Is that sufficient?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one more sentence, Dr. Karadzic. I appreciate your tolerance. Just at the -- or shall I? "[Interpretation] You will now have the opportunity of assessing whether or not my views are something that are -- is acceptable and all right and something that the Assembly stands by, and for me what is particularly important -- something that is particularly important for me and backed up by the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina but by Yugoslavia as well. It's a political and historical equality for Bosnia-Herzegovina as a reality." [In English] So he opens this to questions about what he has just said and asks for inquiries and input in a sense. And I'd like to go down, if I could, one more page and point out that Dr. Karadzic was the next speaker after these words were spoken. Now, I believe that is actually on the next page at the top or -- I'm sorry. It's after this speech. This speech goes on to page 7, 8, 9, and 10. So it's -- it will be five pages down from where we are right now. And below the box that's just been created, you see that Dr. Karadzic makes a brief speech, and he corrects a quote that Mr. Izetbegovic had taken from an interview that Dr. Karadzic had done with the Belgrade newspaper "Borba," but makes no mention of the words that he had just heard from Mr. Izetbegovic. Would you like, Your Honour, to read - it's just about a page - through that speech, or is my, perhaps, testimony to that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If necessary, Ms. Edgerton will take it up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That was precisely what I wanted to say, but I had nothing against it because it's a fact that I always strove for having a federal state and federal laws predominantly. That's what it says here. Thank you. Mr. Donia, do you remember the agreement of the 18th of March? And we'll come back to that later on, but tell me first, did that agreement fulfil Izetbegovic's criterion as expressed here? Or rather, two criteria that he set, an integral and sovereign Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what agreement of 18 March?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The Lisbon Agreement. And all three sides, on the 18th of March, subscribed to it, that Bosnia step down from Yugoslavia, that its borders be kept, that it was integral and sovereign.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you've characterised as the Lisbon Agreement, Dr. Karadzic, was an agreement in principle that was to be the basis for further negotiations, and all three national parties, represented by their leaders, subscribed to the principles but were very careful not to finalise the agreement, including you. You were very explicit that you would not agree to anything that had not been signed, and this document had not been signed. So I would dispute that there was a final agreement on the 18th of March, 1992, and further point out that that is some 14 months, 13 months, after this -- these statements were made by -- by him and by you in the Bosnian Assembly and that much had changed in that period of time. Many other interim agreements in principle had been reached, many of them had been breached and that the situation really was radically altered, both in terms of the situation on the ground and the position of the primary political participants.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, would you agree with me that two questions remain to be addressed, the maps and the question of the army, on the 18th of March, that is. Did we agree that we would continue our discussions about the maps to determine them more precisely, that the basic map was adopted as a starting point, but that what remained was to discuss the map and the question of the army?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The agreement was characterised at the time by you, by the EC negotiators as an agreement in principle as to be the basis for further negotiations. What specific issues were agreed upon and not signed and what remained to be resolved, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But we proclaimed it publicly, that what remained to be done was to define the maps and to resolve the question of the army as a referendum question, that the referendum should confirm the agreement reached. All the principles were adopted. All that remained to be done was the map. The map was adopted as a basis but the issue of the army was left to the end. And that was published, it was made public, completely public?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure there's documentation to the effect of what was announced publicly, and there's plenty of documentation on the character of the agreement in principle in the extensive discussions in the 11th Assembly -- the Bosnian Serb Assembly and in your own statements and the statements of other leaders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was the -- was the minutes -- were the minutes adopted in total or just a part of it because this was a joint Assembly?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are we back in 1991 now in -- in the Assembly that we're looking at?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about this text that you and I have been reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We're talking about a minute which is of 252 pages, but our practice has been to admit it in its entirety. So you'd like to replace this with the previous one which has been already admitted?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what has been admitted so far. The part that I started to read, and Mr. Donia concluded, refers to Mr. Izetbegovic. Of course, I have nothing against the entire minutes be admitted into the file. If that is more convenient for the Chamber, the part which refers to Mr. Izetbegovic's words, what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit it being marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just offer something that might assist --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- the Trial Chamber. Subject to what Dr. Karadzic, of course, and Dr. Donia say, the passage at which President Izetbegovic begins speaking is at page 96 of this 65 ter number 06291, and it ends at page 105. And in terms of the translation issue, perhaps this might assist in providing Your Honours and my colleagues in the courtroom with the appropriate context to be able to evaluate the discussion and not unduly burden anybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And Mr. Karadzic's speech that followed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Which I can check, but I think those are the two pages that follow. So 106 and 107.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I note it's Mr. Krajisnik's speech, albeit brief. With that note, we'll admit it being marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D256, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we now go back, Mr. Donia, to what you said before, that we should establish the causes and the consequences and their mutual relationship. To that effect, do you recall that in the period prior to the elections and up to this moment, up to February 1991, we spoke about communities or municipalities, about the need to set up new communities of municipalities?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There -- yes. There was -- you and the party had discussed communities of municipalities and establishing new communities of municipalities prior to this speech, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that that was based on the constitution?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There -- there is -- there is a part of this question I can't answer, but there was a provision in the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina from 1974 that provided for communities of municipalities to be established with the purpose of aggregating municipalities for certain specific functions. What I don't know is what legislation or other constitutional provisions may have been involved in the creation of such communities and municipalities, whether the republic Assembly had to agree to them, whether the republican -- whether the republic Presidency had to agree to them and what steps were required in order to establish these communities of municipalities. In fact, a number of them existed by 1990, including, significantly, the Banja Luka community of municipalities, which incorporated 12 or 15 municipalities in and around Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we just clarify one thing. You know what the local commune is, of course. Do you agree this is a smaller territorial unit which is comprised within a municipality?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think we can say the smallest administrative unit in the republic, in fact, in most of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that a local commune can comprise several villages, or a large village can comprise a number of local communes?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know what an "atar," which is a village area, is? Is this the territory of a village?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So a local commune can have a number of villages, and every village has its own boundaries with their forest, their woodlands, their meadows. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: A couple questions there. A local commune can include a number of villages. Normally, it did not. Normally, a village was a local commune or "mjesna zajednica," but it could have more. And a large village could consist of several "mjesna zajednica" or local communities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If we imagine the boundary of a village, and the territory is called in our language an "atar," do you agree that during the Communists, such a territory was, for the most part, socially owned property in that period?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. Socially owned, that kind of vague category of land which was not owned by any individual or enterprise but belonged in some sense to the state or to the -- administered often by the local municipality. I concur with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That means that one area, village area, or atar, belonged to that village or to that territorial unit. The socially owned property belonging to that particular territorial unit. Namely, that the villagers of another village were not allowed to fell wood in the atar, or in the district, the area of another village.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that socially owned land, which accounted for probably half, I think a little over half of all of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was indeed socially owned. It was not owned by a village or a municipality or any territorial unit but was defined as socially owned land which was then under the administration, if you will, if those entities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that the Communist regime actually acquired such social ownership of property by actually seizing, appropriating private property, after the revolution?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There certainly was some of that, but this practice of common lands which did not belong to any one person goes back centuries, and existed in the Ottoman period in Bosnia, was a big factor in some of the discussions about land reform in the Austro-Hungarian period, from 1878 to 1918, and also in the time of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia. So as a matter of historical continuity, it had been there a long time, but there were some seizures of property that took place in the five years after 1945.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I just ask for 65 ter 18514. That is the power-sharing criteria for power sharing between these three parties. And can I also ask for a map of Bosnia-Herzegovina with municipal boundaries drawn up. The number of the map is number 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we haven't assigned the number for the documents regarding criteria, so we'll give it number -- marking for identification pending translation of the second page.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That will be MFI D257.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karadzic, for reminding that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we get this map. My marks are 02, namely the second map from 0701 to 0703. That is the Karadzic maps binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, until we see this -- these, do you agree that the seats of communities of municipalities had administrative institutions, such as the public auditing service, the tax administration, the security services centre? In other words, that it was -- that they were states in a nutshell?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what your concept, how you see the seat of community of municipalities?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they certainly had no -- none of the attributes of sovereignty which would make them qualify as a state. I hope there's not a translation problem here, but they were not states. They were typically associations of municipalities created for specific purposes, such as sewer systems and water and in some cases administrative convenience of financial or administrative character. They could indeed have public auditing service units which was actually a powerful financial tool for directing monies. Money didn't pass anywhere in the former Yugoslavia without going through a public auditing service. So the name "Public auditing service" is bit misleading. It's actually much more powerful than just auditing. It's actually a -- almost like a regional bank. So it could have some of those administrative institutions, but it always was a creature of the municipalities that made it up.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I tell you that -- and I believe it that it is Article 52 of the 1955 constitution, which hasn't changed, which said that municipalities had the possibility to pool into municipality communities, and one of those communes would usually be the seat of that community and would contain all these institutions which you, too, have now listed. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please call up this map. Perhaps it is map number 2, and the binder is 0701 to 0723 on e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We can't seem to find, locate, the 65 ter number. I was told that it's time to take a break, and in the meantime we'll be able to see the map through e-court. Twenty-five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, can I ask you to cast a glance at this map and to tell us whether this is a map with the municipal boundaries of Bosnia and Herzegovina drawn in.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that the city of Sarajevo is drawn in as a single entity without the boundaries of the city municipalities indicated?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that appears to be the case.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we scroll it up a bit, please. And a bit more so that we can see Trebinje on the map. And slightly more. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, in the southern-most part we have Trebinje, Ljubinje, Bileca, Nevesinje, and Gacko municipalities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, mm-hmm. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that these are municipalities with a marked Serbian majority?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As -- as I recall, they all have Serbian majorities, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that these are traditionally designated as Eastern Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that as part of Stolac Municipality there is a place which is called Berkovici and which used to be a municipality?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You don't know that, or you deny it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me if I recalled. I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But if I tell you that Berkovici used to be a municipality and was later annexed to Stolac, would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you are actually denying it.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm open to see evidence that that was the case and would welcome doing so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does it sound sensible if I tell you that Berkovici -- the development of Berkovici stopped altogether the moment Berkovici was annexed to Stolac Municipality?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you familiar with the term "gerrymandering"? That is from the American political lingo.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a term from American political corruption, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. Thank you for the explanation. It's put much better. Your formulation is much better. It consists of manipulating electoral districts, constituencies, in order for a minority party to win the elections and win power; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not quite, no. The term "gerrymandering" comes from a governor, Gerry of Massachusetts, in the early 19th century, who redrew electoral districts in such a way to ensure his own re-election, and the district that he drew to ensure his own re-election looked like a salamander on a map, and so the term came to refer to efforts by an existing power holder to assure re-election usually through creating some very odd-shaped collection of electoral stations in order to marginalise or out-vote a certain group of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this explanation. This is what Gerry did, but the gerrymandering phenomenon can be applied to all such kinds of manipulation, can it not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It is specifically a manipulation to ensure re-election.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know to which community of municipalities these Eastern Herzegovina municipalities belong and where the seat is?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What period are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Before the 1990 elections.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would it occur to you that it would be natural for Trebinje to be that seat, which is a well-developed city with a developed industry and would naturally be the seat of those municipalities?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there might be a couple candidates amongst those municipalities that you've mentioned to be the seat of a community of municipalities. I don't know specifically which one was or if there was one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I tell you that all these Serbian municipalities are associated, are linked up, with Mostar as their seat, would it make sense to you that these municipalities had reason for dissatisfaction, because Mostar was rapidly developing at their expense?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've characterised these as Serbian municipalities, and I wouldn't accept that characterisation. They, in fact, all had mixed populations. They did indeed have Serb majority populations, but the towns, in particular, had quite diverse populations, at least most of them did, and had their -- it was as a unit a somewhat distinctive economic category or type of area which it was quite rural and fairly rocky terrain, a lot of agricultural productivity in it. I don't know why Mostar would be logical or illogical as a seat of a community of associations that included these municipalities. Mostar, of course, is the most important, largest city in this part of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It's -- it had been at that time quite economically developed, very mixed population in terms of both class and ethnicity, so would be certainly a strong candidate to be a suitable centre for such a community -- or association of municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is not New York a good candidate for a capital of New York State, and Albany is, actually, the capital? Why would Mostar be developing at a rapid pace and Trebinje be lagging behind? Do you believe that to be a democratic gain, a democratic achievement?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't accept that Mostar was developing faster than Trebinje. I don't have the numbers of or economic metrics to know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can live with that, but I should like to put the following fact to you: These municipalities have a population which is over 80 per cent majority Serbian. Their development was totally slowed down, not to say stopped, over a number of decades. Do you think that a seat of financial power and of administrative power, of economic power, investment power which was in Mostar, if it had been in Bileca or Trebinje, would it have had an impact on the development of this entire region?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's a rather socialist way of thinking about it. I really don't think that the issue of, let's say, putting the seat one place or the other is not necessarily going to make an impact on the development of the region. There very well could be that the most financially and administratively developed seat would be the most desirable, because it could take advantage of all the resources available to a somewhat larger city in order to develop the entire region. So I don't accept the premise that if you just plunked the seat of a community of municipalities in a remote area that it would automatically lead to economic development.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Trebinje is not in a remote area. It is the centre of Herzegovina. Are you contesting the fact that Eastern Herzegovina developed at a slower pace than Mostar, as also had other regions in the Neretva River valley?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying I don't know. I don't have the -- I'm sure that's a very knowable fact based on economic indicators. I don't have those economic indicators at hand, nor do I have an active recollection of looking at them and so I can't answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I hope that next week I will be able to show you something, some of these things. Did you encircle on this map the boundaries of these municipalities towards Trebinje -- or could you. Could you. Could you please encircle on this map the boundaries of these municipalities.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What? I'm sorry, what are you asking?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you draw a circle round the Serb community of municipalities moving towards Mostar. Just draw them in, mark them. The boundaries of Gacko, Nevesinje, up to Mostar, those municipalities. Circle them, to Stolac and so on.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't -- I haven't agreed that there was a community of municipalities of Eastern Herzegovina. I have not seen evidence that there was or when it was created or anything of the kind or what municipalities made it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, if that was your purpose, we can see -- the Judges can see the map ourselves. We can see where Mostar is, and we can see all the municipalities you referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, but do you agree that these municipalities belong to the community of municipalities of Mostar? That's common knowledge. It was generally known.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you see the municipalities of Foca, Gorazde, Cajnice, Rudo, Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you agree that that's what we call Old or Ancient Herzegovina? The other part was Eastern Herzegovina, and this is Old Herzegovina, the area from which I originate, as I said earlier on.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know where the seat of this community of municipalities was?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the -- that there was a community of municipalities. I don't know -- I know there were communities of municipalities prior to 1990. I know approximately which ones belong to the Banja Luka community of municipalities, but exactly what municipalities were members of the others and where their seats were, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I tell you that the seat of this community of municipalities was in Gorazde, which was predominantly Muslim, and not in Foca, which is larger and more developed and which was populated by a Serb majority until recently or an equal ratio of the population, what would you have to say to that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd want to see the documentation on its creation and see, in fact, what the seat was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you would have to know that. It's the subject of your expert report. You must know that, because it's a question of the political history of the Bosnian crisis. If in your report you object to Karadzic's position whereby the municipalities were re-partitioned, then you'd have to seek the reasons for that, why Karadzic was asking for that. My case is that Gorazde developed in an accelerated fashion compared to Foca, and especially Cajnice, which was became -- was desperate, and Rudo too, because the seat of that community of municipalities and all the institutions, political, economic, financial power, was situated in Gorazde, and that's what I'm putting to you. That's my case in this particular point, and that's why we asked for a reorganisation of the municipalities based on the constitution. Do you consider that -- do you not consider that you should have checked out what it was that Karadzic was asking for if you objected to his proposals? Shouldn't you have looked into the matter?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I, Dr. Karadzic, described your general critique of the municipal structure. I think I described it fairly. I did not go into the individual municipal situations other than mentioning, I think, Ozren, which you mention numerous times in your speeches and articles and interviews. I, frankly, have not heard you make this case before, and I am not convinced it is the case that the seat of a community of municipalities would far outstrip in development the other municipal seats of municipalities that are a part of that community. First time I've heard you make it and I would certainly need to be convinced that that's the case. And I think to do that you would have to look at all the communities of municipalities and see what happened to their seats over several decades, because the thesis is not self-evident, not self-evidently true that you would get a rapid economic growth of a single administrative centre of such a relatively thin administrative level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. We'll show that in due course and we'll come to Ozren, too.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But can we move the map down a bit now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you see where it says Srebrenica and Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, Srebrenica and Bratunac, do they resemble a salamander?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. That's -- that's a judgement call. I don't. I don't see a salamander, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, with respect to gerrymandering, you mentioned salamander, and if I tell you that at the top of that horn you have Skelani, which would have developed quite properly had they been given the territories which belonged to them, and the municipalities of Srebrenica and Bratunac were distorted in this way. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you know that Skelani was a municipality at one time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you see Lopare, Ugljevik? Do you know that's where Mount Majevica is?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on Serb territory there was a municipality called Priboj, and now we can't even find Priboj on the map.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean by "Serb territory"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, that area was populated 100 per cent by Serbs. That's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What area was that again?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The -- well, Mount Majevica, Lopare, Ugljevik, that area, moving towards Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know the exact composition of those municipalities in 1991, but I do know that none of them were a hundred per cent Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, was Bosnia 100 per cent Muslim?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How, then, can we justify attempts to have Bosnia become independent when it's not even 50 per cent Muslim, whereas here your criterion is you're questioning Majevica as being 100 per cent Serb? Priboj was almost 80 per cent Serb and the municipality was abolished.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I note you've exaggerated the number or the percentage in the first time you asked me the question. Now you've come down to say it's almost 80 per cent. So your representations here are inconsistent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, what I'm going to say is that it's not essential how much over 50 per cent, but the fact is that Priboj was a municipality, whereas now I have to use a magnifying glass to find it. It's to the southern reaches of Ugljevik, and it's died a natural death. There's nothing there anymore. It's a very small place now because the municipal seat was abolished and joined to the neighbouring municipalities. So do you consider or do you think that the municipality never existed at Majevica?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do I think that the municipality never existed at Majevica? I don't think you've even suggested there was a municipality at Majevica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The Priboj municipality on Mount Majevica. Now, do you agree, Mr. Donia, that municipalities in the world range from 1.500 to 5.000 inhabitants as a general rule?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The municipalities in the world?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In most countries in the world.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the average population of municipalities in the Soviet Union and Yugoslavia was 40.000? In all other countries the figure was less.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's about the average in Bosnia. I -- or was the average in -- in about 1991. I don't know about Soviet Union.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was around 40.000. And do you know that in other countries the number of inhabitants is significantly lower? For example, Greece has 8.500 on an average. All the rest have less than that. Are you aware of that? Is that something you know about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How is it assisting the Chamber, Mr. Karadzic? Let's move on to your next question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you'll see, Your Excellencies, that gerrymandering and the manipulation -- manipulations with the population and municipalities is a pre-eminently political category and that that's what led to the crisis. But never mind, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Donia, do you see the municipality of Bijeljina, Ugljevik, Lopare, Zvornik? Do you see those municipalities?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zvornik, Lopare. I'm sorry, what was the other one? Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Bijeljina and Ugljevik. Do you agree that Bijeljina, Ugljevik and Lopare belong to Semberija and Majevica? Semberija and Majevica, that general area.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're using the term geographically, yes, that would be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know where their seat was, the community of municipalities, I mean?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, I don't know the precise communities of municipalities that existed prior to 1990. I know that not all municipalities belonged to a community of municipalities, and I furthermore don't know where their seats were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what was the regional centre of these municipalities? Perhaps you'll find it easier to answer that way. Do you agree that the regional centre of these municipalities was Tuzla and not Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And if I tell you that it was Tuzla and that Tuzla had an accelerated development and that it wasn't Bijeljina and that Bijeljina is just beginning to develop now, what would you have to say to that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's the case, but the reasons for the accelerated development of Tuzla didn't have anything to do with municipal -- being the seat of a community of municipalities. To my knowledge, Tuzla really grew upon its salt deposits and the substantial industrialisation that was put there, including the soda chemical plant and other facilities that were developed in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And how do you now explain the fact that Bijeljina is flourishing although it went through the war and sanctions and poverty, that suddenly Bijeljina is flourishing and developing because it's now the regional centre?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've been to Bijeljina but I saw it as actually having developed in the socialist period a great deal. I wouldn't agree with the characterisation. Again, it may be some numbers that -- some economic metrics that can establish this, but it's a place that's grown rather dramatically, I think, under socialism. In fact, that whole strip along the Drina River there is actually developed a great deal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And if I tell you that Bijeljina started developing after this latest war, the civil war, our war, when it became a regional centre and that everything is flourishing there, how else could you explain that but to say that income from Bijeljina no longer goes to Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think you're wrong about, really, the trajectory of development throughout the socialist period. I understand that you have plenty of reasons to be unhappy with Communists and Socialists, including some very personal reasons, but I think you have to acknowledge that the development of Bosnia-Herzegovina under socialism was enormous, particularly in the first 30 years of -- of socialism, and that virtually every city grew larger. The economy really prospered. Industrialisation was widespread, population increased and became more literate. So those are all simply facts of the era of economic development under socialism. So I'd submit that you probably can't find much of a town that didn't at one time or another prosper more so than it had in earlier decades under socialism.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you consider that the development of Bosnia-Herzegovina was regionally well balanced, and did you see in our platform the call for a well-balanced regional development? That was one of the points in the platform of the Serbian Democratic Party. Just take it one by one. Did you notice in our programme or platform the call for equitable regional development or well-balanced regional development?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you claim that a well-balanced regional development existed in Bosnia-Herzegovina? Before these elections, I mean.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it depends on how you define the regions. The -- certainly the development in the Sarajevo area was probably the most dramatic and the greatest. There were other areas that didn't industrialise at the rate of Sarajevo, and, in fact, most regions probably didn't industrialise at the rate Sarajevo did. But in general, I think the -- I haven't seen evidence to suggest that regions, whole regions, were dramatically backward relative to the rest of the republic. I remember when the Banja Luka leadership started to organise the community of municipalities of Bosanska Krajina. The principal promoter of that project was Dr. Dusko Jaksic, who was then the director of the economic institute in Banja Luka. As far as I know, he still is. And when that political demand arose for -- to correct the backwardness of Bosnian Krajina, he, who was the principal promoter of the idea, frankly told interlocutors that there were no numbers to show that. So I think it -- it remains in my mind to be established that there was this discrimination against regions or backwardness of regions based on some political criterion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, we'll come to that Mr. Donia, but do you see Gracanica, Lukavac, Maglaj, Zavidovici, Banovici, and those two rivers there, to the left is the River Bosna, passing through Maglaj, and to the right is Braca, which goes from Lukavac, Gracanica, and they -- their confluence is in Doboj.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think we probably just lost everybody else in the room, but I know what area you're speaking of, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, in between these two rivers, is Mount Ozren there between those two rivers?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, do you know that up on Mount Ozren there was a municipality at one time called Petrovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't -- didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that that municipality was abolished and Ozren, which was 100 per cent Serb, inhabited by Serbs, was divided up among the neighbouring Muslim municipalities?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I object to your characterisation of the neighbouring municipalities as Muslim, and I don't know the administrative history of that -- of the Ozren area prior to 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What I'm trying to say, Mr. Donia, this is something that every peasant there knows, namely, that their lives and development virtually ceased when the municipality of Petrovo was abolished. Now they again have that municipality. Municipality of Petrovo and Ozren, as an area, were divided among the other municipalities in each of which the Serbs became a national minority. Did you know -- do you know why I'm talking about Ozren as a paradigm, not as Ozren in its own right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're talking about Ozren as a paradigm? I'm -- what do you mean by that? I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What I'm saying, that a compact Serbian entity was abolished as a municipality and was divided among the other municipalities, the adjacent neighbouring municipalities, in which the Serbs became a minority.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Well, first of all, that's not gerrymandering because there was no anticipation of elections at the time the administrative boundaries were drawn. I take it what you have done is gerrymandering, in the wartime period and immediately afterwards, to assure Serb parties would -- would prevail in those areas. The -- if you look at the distribution of Serb villages that I've looked at around the -- just south of Doboj in that Ozren area, what you get is indeed a serpentine kind of configuration, and to look at those villages as a municipality would be contrary to the whole notion of a municipality as it existed under socialism and which I explained a couple of days ago, which was a municipality was to have a centre, a seat, bearing the same name as the municipality. It was to be as economically self-sufficient as possible. It would be surrounded by land that is partly agricultural, partly simply socially owned land that would be essentially free space and suburban villages, and the purpose of that notion of a municipality was, in fact, geographic and economic. It was designed to encourage economic development, and that is the level at which economic development was encouraged under socialism. The communities of municipalities were incidental to that fundamental unit of analysis or administration which, as you know, became a socio-political community in the definition of socialist-era constitutions. So I understand your -- your critique of -- and your use of Ozren in particular as an example of this, but I do believe that if you actually made a municipality out of Ozren, it would be largely ethnically homogenous and would probably defeat the possibility of economic development because it would be so geographically contorted and not have the diversity that one would look for in a developing region like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you agree with me that in a democracy the people should have been asked what it was that they wanted.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a general principle, I would agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we take a look at Western Bosnia. You see Bosanski Petrovac, Titov Drvar, Bosansko Grahovo, and Glamoc. Do you know where the seat was, to which community of municipalities did Bosanski Petrovac and Drvar belong?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you talking about the period before 1990? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Their seat was at Bihac, and those municipalities were devastated. The people left. There was no industry. There was no economy. The people abandoned the area. Do you believe me or should I give you the figures?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'd love to see the figures. I do want to point out that in this case one is dealing with an administrative centre that had been an administrative centre for that part of Bosnia going back well over a hundred years. So -- and the same would be true of -- of Mostar. When the Austrian -- Austro-Hungarian administrators came in, they selected basically the five or six largest towns to be administrative centres in somewhat the same spirit as municipalities were later created under the socialist government. So the -- again, the argument you're making here is not to me at all self-evident, that purely dumping a -- making a place an administrative centre would result in a flourishing economy or in outstripping other areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, Mr. Donia, a million and a half Serbs are listening to this, and three million Muslims and Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina, they know exactly what I'm talking about. Where there is the administrative centre of a community of municipalities, there you have the economic power, the money, the finance, the investments. Everything is there, and everything from the pertaining municipalities go there. Do you know that Glamoc and Bosansko Grahovo were linked up with Livno, and that Glamoc and Bosansko Grahovo lagged behind tremendously in their development whereas Bosansko Grahovo did not -- sorry, whereas Livno did not.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you've just overestimated our listening and watching audience by about 4.5 million, but the economic development of these areas I -- I don't pretend to know the relative economic development of each, and I'm not convinced that the, let's say, differential development of one city to another is based on whether it's the seat of a municipality -- community of municipalities or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that before the Second World War, Kalinovik had 25.000 inhabitants, and before this war 5.000 inhabitants? Kalinovik is a predominantly Serb municipality between Foca and Kalinovik.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with either -- the population at either time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Between Foca and Nevesinje. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, you have stated your position vis-a-vis our political view that communities of municipalities were -- are just and detrimental [as interpreted] from the economic standpoint to us, that the motives of those who did this were ethnocentric. Do you agree with me that you had to know these things that I'm asking you about in order to draw such a conclusion, namely, that the Serbs were making some demands about municipality boundaries which actually were not justified? And we see that those boundaries changed, and they changed because of the moves made by the Communists.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there's about five questions there, and I'm going to try and sort them out. You state that I expressed the viewpoint that the motives of those who did this were ethnocentric. I did not make that statement. I have looked --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I was not precise myself. You -- you said that our demand encroaching upon the municipalities or the communities of municipalities was some sort of a politically subversive action, something which was not desirable and was not justified. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think that's correct. I noted your critique of the municipal structure and stated that -- I mean, I've looked at Sarajevo more than anyplace else, and I also looked at Bosnian Krajina to some degree, and based on looking at those areas, I did not see an ethno-national factor in the determinations of municipal boundaries under socialism, and I think I indicated that in the main, or for all practical purposes or something like that, the drawing of municipal boundaries was not driven by ethnicity, and I stand by that. I think the municipal boundaries that we're looking at today were basically created with the intent of having rational economic development units within geographically manageable administrative areas. And there were other factors that went into those boundaries. The fact of the matter is that developing 109 municipalities is an extraordinary undertaking for a government, any government, and is probably about the lowest unit that one could realistically expect to have an impact on in terms of economic development. And even then, a lot of those -- you can go into any one of these municipalities even today and see factories, some of them abandoned, some of them very small, that were put there during the socialist period to try to contribute to the economic self-sufficiency of municipalities. I would point out that you are looking at this from a strictly national viewpoint, strictly ethnic viewpoint, and you're tying those proposals to your claims of Serb land, and that's fine. I am not saying that's illegal to advocate or even to ultimately achieve. I'm not making that judgement, but I am pointing out that it is linked to your understanding of what Serb land is and that the municipality redesign that you have in mind would, in fact, be gerrymandering in creating solid Serb areas that would be overwhelmingly Serbian composition, leaving the rest aside.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you for saying that this is a legal and legitimate thing, but this is not how I read it in your paper. But let me ask you this: Who would actually have endured it if municipality -- the municipality of Berkovici continued to exist? To whose detriment would that be if the municipality of Petrovo, on Ozren, continued to exist, and other municipalities? Who would that -- who would be -- have been hurt by that? Why would it have been detrimental to anyone?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I take it, then, you're proposing to re-establish those now long-gone municipalities? Is that what you're proposing?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, they were established. Berkovici exist again. Petrovo exists once more. And the people, the community, now has its income, and they continue to develop. They can have their own school now. They can have their own development, which was arrested when those municipalities were abolished. Now, do you believe, justified or not, that in socialism it was very important where the SDK, the social accounting service, was, where the bank was, where the Municipal Committee was, the inter-municipal committee of the League of Communists was seated, where the self-management community of interest was? You know what the SIZ, the self-management community of interest, was, for health, for education and so on. So all these financial institutions which had their hands on the income of the entire community. Do you agree that under socialism, that was concentrated in the seats of these communities of municipalities?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, where, then, were these institutions if not in this community of municipalities and their seats?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, many of them were municipal-level institutions, and I think you're attributing too much grandeur to the communities of municipalities that existed under socialism.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And why then -- why did this become important -- we wanted to redesign the community of municipalities?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it became important because you adopted it as a tool to weaken, cripple, and eventually disable the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. You used it as a state-building tool for the rudiments of a new Bosnian Serb polity with the intent of superseding Bosnia-Herzegovina as it existed in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you mean to say that we intended to create a Serb state in Bosnia in July 1990, when we formed the party and set out the party programme?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't mean to say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But at the time, we had criticisms of regional development. Do you accept that our motive was regional development, which in the Serb lands was lagging behind because the incomes of those regions were placed in the hands of the centres which did not belong to those areas but exploited them. Simply speaking, those areas were exploited.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, the things that you did in the early 1990s set the economic development of Bosnia back 50 years. You destroyed the economy. You destroyed the infrastructure that it was dependent upon, and to suggest that this now has turned into a situation of economic prosperity after the war in Republika Srpska is to me just an implausible assertion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ah, well, Mr. Donia, you have now expanded my task. I now have this question to ask you: Did we, in 1990, even think of regionalisation? Did it enter our head at all?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. The first activities in favour of regionalisation I can see on -- in mid-January 1991. So whether this occurred to you as a -- as a project, that is, to form regional associations based on the SDS initiative, whether that occurred to you in 1990, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But let's stick to what all of us can know, and that is that our pre-election campaign was that the boundaries of the municipalities and the communities of municipalities should be adapted to the wishes and needs of the democratically -- the democratic intentions of the population living there and the population who wanted to live better, have a better life, and that there was no question of any autonomous regions in Bosnia-Herzegovina; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I note several questions here. Certainly the proposal to redraw municipal boundaries was a part of the pre-election campaign. I didn't see much evidence that it was linked to the economic dimension in the course of the campaign. You clearly had one or two points in your platform that were contributed or devoted to economic development, but very little of that then actually found its way beyond maybe the first few weeks of the campaign and was pretty well forgotten about after the campaign was over. I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since this map has not got any markings on it we won't be tendering. May we have D255 next, please, which was already an exhibit, just to show you that Mr. Izetbegovic had set out before him in our platform -- well, that the SDA never had any criticism to make about those activities of ours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have D255 next, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So that we can establish, Mr. Donia, when it was that the Serbs found the need to create autonomous regions and when they found the need to create Republika Srpska, because without them we cannot make these sweeping statements. Now, look at the last paragraph there: "Everywhere, especially here in Bosnia-Herzegovina, we were for the most part devoted to the system which seemed to have been established to ensure our national annihilation. In the time of the greatest devotion to the regime and the system, the greatest impoverishment occurred precisely in those devoted Serbian areas, and Serbian areas loyal to the system were the very ones to suffer economic and cultural decline and large-scale migration. Several hundred thousand Serbs left Bosnia and Herzegovina in this period, and Bosnia and Herzegovina was left without their progeny. Territorial organisation broke down the natural Serbian entities in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the Serbian nation was reduced to an inferior economic, demographic, and political position." This is an extract taken from a speech, the introductory speech at the founding Assembly, my speech, and nobody had anything to say about that because it can be borne up -- it can be substantiated by any economic analysis. Do you agree with that, Mr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I noted earlier that my concern with your speech at the founding Assembly was the degree to which you had already formulated this notion of a Serb people as a homogenous whole and coherent population group, and this is what I had in mind. The notion that Serbs were the victim of the socialist period just to me is counter intuitive. It misstates the whole character of the socialist government and its -- its intentions and its policies. I think that actually one later in the campaign more commonly heard the proposition that the government had, in fact, retarded the economic development of all three peoples in that period when you and others were holding the joint rallies amongst the various parties. So I -- I think you're expressing here a kernel of an idea that developed much later and much more, let's say, convincingly, if you will -- not convincingly but tied to a specific programme which was designed to remedy this, but that specific programme was, in fact, based on a single party and mono-ethnic initiative that took wing in 1991. It wasn't, to my mind, there as a specific proposal or initiative in the time of the electoral campaign or even in the few weeks after the election, but it did have its origins in -- in early 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, do you consider that the Serb people did not exist as an entity but that I tried to create it? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say you tried to create it. I'd say you looked at it as a kind of national revival. You were trying to raise the consciousness, the national consciousness of those people who could potentially think of themselves as Serbs, and perhaps for one -- one or another reason describe their identity as hybrid or as Yugoslav or as something else, and you wanted those people to think of themselves as Serbs and to behave as Serb nationalists at -- which meant embracing the ideals and programme of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we see page 3 of this same document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, do you think that the Serbs in Bosnia should have been something other than the Serbs in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think they were different from Serbs east of the Drina in certain limited ways. Their situation was different. They were involved in the lives of other republics and had specific ideals that appealed to them, although I think in general the Serb -- let's say, Serb national leaders shared many ideals and many -- and Serbs share the same basic allegiance to their national identity. But there were some differences, and I think -- I personally find those very interesting. I think the -- one of them was that Serbs west of the Drina seem to be more oriented to the Serb experience in the Second World War than did Serbs in Serbia proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you agree that the Serbs from Nis and the Serbs from Novi Sad are different among themselves than the Serbs from Bosnia and Sumadija?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think you could think of them as, if you will, subcommunities of a broader national community of people who shared the Serb identity in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What I'm concerned about, Mr. Donia, is this: You seem to consider that we generated something in Bosnia-Herzegovina which we did not have the right to. Do a million and a half Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina have the right to fight for their economic -- well, for their equality, equality with others, for their economic prosperity, cultural identity, and national identity? Do they -- this collective of a million and a half people, do they have their rights, the rights to do that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think all people have the rights that you basically described, all citizens of any polity should have those rights. They do not have the right to -- should not have the right to eliminate those of other groups from territories that they claim or claim huge blocks of territory which are to be devoid of those that are currently living there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you making a judgement, then? Are you saying that the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina wanted to do that, wanted to do it that way?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm simply saying that they have a lot of rights, should have those rights, along with other citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They should have those same rights as other citizens have, but that when it comes to destroying other -- the basis of other groups, that they should not have those rights, and neither should any another group.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, all right. We'll come to that. But are you suggesting that's what the Serbs did? Is that your position, that the Serbs did what you said they did and that which they should not have done?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, talking about the period that -- let me make clear. Talking about the period that we're talking about, which is prior to January 1991, absolutely not. I am not making that suggestion. I think if you get into 1992, much of that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We will clarify that in due course, but, Mr. Donia, do you think that the formation of the Croatian Democratic Union, the Croatian Party of Rights, the Party of Democratic Action, did it have some other root but the ethnic root, which you do not allow for the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So all those parties which started out in 1990, mostly in the west, had -- well, the main parties that won the elections both in Slovenia and Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina had an ethnic motive, an ethno-democratic stream, motive.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- there was, as I discussed yesterday, to me a fluorescence of democratic national activity going back to very late 1989, when it became evident that multi-party elections would be held in Bosnia and in Yugoslavia in some form. Part of that activity, much of that activity, fluorescence, if you will, took place in support of the formation of national parties. Some of it was non-national. Some of it could even be called anti-national, but it was a product of the arrival of democracy. And so people formed parties by the dozens and hundreds in the former Yugoslavia at that time and their nature and programmes were as diverse as one could find in a -- in a newly emerging democracy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that the Croatian Democratic Union as a predominantly national party in Croatia quite literally wiped out all the other parties? It had a major victory. That's my first question. Yes or no. That will suffice.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Wiped out other parties? No. It did not wipe out other parties. It had a victory which was actually less than an absolute majority in the elections because of the -- but won the majority of seats because of the first-past-the-post system that had been voted into effect by the outgoing Communist-dominated legislature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the Croatian voters had an alternative. They had others to vote for, but they opted for the HDZ. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I just said that they -- the HDZ did not receive a majority of the votes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I think that they won most of the seats, but I think we also agree that the Party of Democratic Action was formed before the Serbian Democratic Party. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I indicated that if you look -- if you -- if the measure that you'd like to use to recognise parties as having organised is their founding Assemblies, that the Party of Democratic Action was formed in -- on May 26 and the SDS was formed in early July. There are other measures that one could use. I think that's a reasonable one to use, and if you'll agree that that's the reasonable one to use, then it would be the case that the SDA was formed before the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can anybody in the world claim that the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina would have formed the Serbian Democratic Party had all that not been preceded by the superior or significant victory of the HDZ in Croatia, the HDZ activity in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Party of Democratic Action's formation? Do you think that the SDS would ever have been formed had these others not previously been formed? Do you have a shred of evidence to prove that that would not have happened?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you're asking me to prove a negative, but I would point out, as I did yesterday, that there was a great deal of organising activity going on, at least starting with the first month of 1990, that eventually culminated in the organisation of the SDS. I think that the specific form that the SDS took was a product of a number of factors. One was the recognition by yourself and others that to form the party as an affiliate of a party in a neighbouring republic was ill-advised. The HDZ, of course, did that, and I think was not a particularly successful thing to do. Also, your own hesitancy to get involved in -- as president of the party certainly played a part in the specific form that the SDS eventually took, and perhaps significantly the advice of Mr. Cosic and others which kept the SDS in Croatia from becoming the parent of the SDS in Bosnia, which could then be formed as a separate distinct body from the party that Mr. -- Dr. Raskovic was heading in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, we'll adjourn there for today and for this week. So over the weekend plan and think about your -- the remaining of your cross-examination and plan your conduct so as to be able to pose more precise and focused questions, thereby shortening your overall cross-examination time. On Monday we'll be hearing -- we will be sitting in the morning in Courtroom I, but given that there will be a Judges' Plenary at 1.00, so we will adjourn at 10 to 1.00. So I'm telling you for the purpose of your planning. And if necessary, we'll go back -- we'll go into private session and then we can discuss it in the absence of the witness, but there's a motion regarding a witness who will be coming end of this month, and now I'm wondering whether the Defence is minded to respond to that motion or -- or it is minded to object to it? Can I know in advance?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Actually, Dr. Karadzic and I haven't yet had a chance to discuss that, but we can let you know tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you do that in writing tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I wish you all have a good rest over the weekend. Monday, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 7th day of June, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.05 p.m.,
